items.readable_text:
Content:
Recall the following theorem, which allows us to compare the cardinality of a finite set to its power set:

Content:
> If [MATH: A] is a finite set such that [MATH: |A| = n,] then [MATH: |\mathcal P(A)| = 2^n.]

Content:
This implies that the power set of [MATH: A] is always larger than [MATH: A.]

Content:
A somewhat analogous theorem, known as Cantor's theorem, allows us to compare the cardinality of an infinite set with its power set. It states the following:

Content:
> The power set of a set [MATH: A] has a larger cardinality than [MATH: A{:}]
> [MATH: |A| \lt |\mathcal{P}(A)|]

Content:
An immediate consequence of Cantor's theorem is that a "largest" cardinality does not exist! Given an infinite set [MATH: A,] we can always construct a set with a larger cardinality, namely [MATH: \mathcal{P}(A).]

Content:
A chain of sets with increasing infinite cardinalities can be obtained by starting with a countably infinite set (for example, [MATH: \mathbb{N}]), and taking its power set, then the power set of the power set, and so on:

Content:
[MATH: \underbrace{|\mathbb{N}|}_{\large \aleph_0} < \underbrace{\big| \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N}) \big|}_{\large \mathfrak{c}} < \underbrace{\big| \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})) \big|}_{\large 2^{\mathfrak{c}}} < \ldots]

Content:
Note that,

Content:
- the cardinality of [MATH: \mathbb{N}] is [MATH: \aleph_0] (countably infinite),
- the cardinality of [MATH: \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})] is [MATH: 2^{\aleph_0}=\mathfrak{c}] (continuum), and
- the cardinality of [MATH: \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})) = \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})] is denoted [MATH: 2^{\mathfrak{c}}.]

Given that [MATH: A = \{ x \in \mathbb{R} \, : \, x^2 <4 \},] which of the following statements are true?

  1. [MATH: \big|\mathcal{P}(A)\big| > \aleph_0]

  2. [MATH: \big|\mathcal{P}(A)\big|> \mathfrak{c}]

  3. [MATH: \big|\mathcal{P}(A)\big| = 2^{\mathfrak{c}}]
sections.readable_text:
Given that [MATH: A = \{ x \in \mathbb{R} \, : \, x^2 <4 \},] which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: \big|\mathcal{P}(A)\big| > \aleph_0]
2. [MATH: \big|\mathcal{P}(A)\big|> \mathfrak{c}]
3. [MATH: \big|\mathcal{P}(A)\big| = 2^{\mathfrak{c}}]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, let's solve the restricting inequality for [MATH: x.] Notice that

[MATH: x^{2}|= 4; x^{2} − 4|= 0; (x + 2)(x − 2)|= 0.]

So, the roots are [MATH: x=-2] and [MATH: x=2,] and we can graph the parabola as follows:

Therefore, the solution to the inequality for [MATH: x \in \mathbb{R}] is

[MATH: -2 < x < 2.]

So, [MATH: A = (-2, 2).] This set has the cardinality of the continuum, i.e., [MATH: |A| = \mathfrak{c}.]

With this in mind, let's examine our statements.

  • Statements I and II are true. According to Cantor's theorem, we have that [MATH: \big| \mathcal{P}(A) \big| > |A| = \mathfrak{c} > \aleph_0.]

  • Statement III is true. Recall that [MATH: |A| = \mathfrak{c}.] So, we have that
    [MATH: \big|\mathcal{P}(A)\big|= 2^{\mathfrak{c}}.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II and III."

As we know, [MATH: \aleph_0] is the "smallest" infinite cardinality, and [MATH: \aleph_0 < \mathfrak{c}.] But is there a set whose cardinality lies strictly between [MATH: \aleph_0] and [MATH: \mathfrak{c}?] In other words, is there a set [MATH: X] such that

Content:

Content:
The assertion that no such set exists is called the continuum hypothesis.

Content:
It may surprise you that neither the continuum hypothesis nor its negation can be proved using the so-called standard axioms of set theory!

Content:
The challenge isn't that mathematicians can't prove the hypothesis because it's too difficult. Instead, a rigorous mathematical proof exists that neither the continuum hypothesis nor its negation can be proved!

Content:
This result might initially appear as a fundamental flaw in the very basics of mathematics. Although it might be unsettling, it's not the end of the world! Instead, it's the birth of two new worlds. This means that the continuum hypothesis (or its negation) should be taken as yet another axiom (a statement that we accept without proof). We do this in math quite often, especially at the beginning of any subject. An example from Euclidian geometry is the statement that exactly one line passes through two distinct points.

Content:
We obtain one mathematical framework if we accept the continuum hypothesis (CH) as true. If we assume the hypothesis is false (so, its negation is true), we arrive at a slightly different mathematical framework. However, both of these "mathematical worlds" are logically consistent. Most of the theorems in both worlds will remain the same, except for statements closely related to the continuum hypothesis. Whatever "world" we choose, it doesn't affect most things people want from math.

Assuming that precisely one straight line passes through a point outside another line and is parallel to it, we get the "standard" Euclidean geometry in the plane. If we assume there can be infinitely many such parallel lines, we get hyperbolic geometry. And, if we assume there are no such parallel lines, we get spherical geometry. All three of these geometries are valid and have applications in different situations.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Recall the following theorem, which allows us to compare the cardinality of a finite set to its power set:

Content:
> If [MATH: A] is a finite set such that [MATH: |A| = n,] then [MATH: |\mathcal P(A)| = 2^n.]

Content:
This implies that the power set of [MATH: A] is always larger than [MATH: A.]

Content:
A somewhat analogous theorem, known as Cantor's theorem, allows us to compare the cardinality of an infinite set with its power set. It states the following:

Content:
> The power set of a set [MATH: A] has a larger cardinality than [MATH: A{:}]
> [MATH: |A| \lt |\mathcal{P}(A)|]

Content:
An immediate consequence of Cantor's theorem is that a "largest" cardinality does not exist! Given an infinite set [MATH: A,] we can always construct a set with a larger cardinality, namely [MATH: \mathcal{P}(A).]

Content:
A chain of sets with increasing infinite cardinalities can be obtained by starting with a countably infinite set (for example, [MATH: \mathbb{N}]), and taking its power set, then the power set of the power set, and so on:

Content:
[MATH: \underbrace{|\mathbb{N}|}_{\large \aleph_0} < \underbrace{\big| \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N}) \big|}_{\large \mathfrak{c}} < \underbrace{\big| \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})) \big|}_{\large 2^{\mathfrak{c}}} < \ldots]

Content:
Note that,

Content:
- the cardinality of [MATH: \mathbb{N}] is [MATH: \aleph_0] (countably infinite),
- the cardinality of [MATH: \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})] is [MATH: 2^{\aleph_0}=\mathfrak{c}] (continuum), and
- the cardinality of [MATH: \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})) = \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})] is denoted [MATH: 2^{\mathfrak{c}}.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Applying Cantor's Theorem

Example Prompt:
Given that [MATH: A = \{ x \in \mathbb{R} \, : \, x^2 <4 \},] which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: \big|\mathcal{P}(A)\big| > \aleph_0]
2. [MATH: \big|\mathcal{P}(A)\big|> \mathfrak{c}]
3. [MATH: \big|\mathcal{P}(A)\big| = 2^{\mathfrak{c}}]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, let's solve the restricting inequality for [MATH: x.] Notice that

[MATH: x^{2}|= 4; x^{2} − 4|= 0; (x + 2)(x − 2)|= 0.]

So, the roots are [MATH: x=-2] and [MATH: x=2,] and we can graph the parabola as follows:

[IMG: /graphics/fde7a51ea7cefdb946897986ee549705]

Therefore, the solution to the inequality for [MATH: x \in \mathbb{R}] is

[MATH: -2 < x < 2.]

So, [MATH: A = (-2, 2).] This set has the cardinality of the continuum, i.e., [MATH: |A| = \mathfrak{c}.]

With this in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statements I and II are true. According to Cantor's theorem, we have that
[MATH: \big| \mathcal{P}(A) \big| > |A| = \mathfrak{c} > \aleph_0.]
- Statement III is true. Recall that [MATH: |A| = \mathfrak{c}.] So, we have that
[MATH: \big|\mathcal{P}(A)\big|= 2^{\mathfrak{c}}.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II and III."

Content:
Recall that the set containing all functions from a set [MATH: X] to a set [MATH: Y] is denoted [MATH: Y^X.] Similar to how [MATH: Y^{\mathbb{N}}] is simply a shortcut for

Content:
[MATH: ℵ_{0}]

we can view [MATH: Y^X] as a shorthand for the Cartesian product of [MATH: Y] with itself [MATH: |X|] times. Note that the cardinality of [MATH: X] here can be finite or infinite (countable or uncountable).

Content:
For example, the set
[MATH: \{ 0,1 \}^{[2,5)}]

Content:

Explanation:

Also, note that [MATH: 2^{\aleph_0} = \mathfrak{c}.]

Therefore, we have

[MATH: |P((0, 1)) × P(N)||= max{|P((0, 1))|,|P(N)|}; = max{2^{c}, 2^{ℵ_{0}}}; = max{2^{c}, c}; = 2^{c}.]

Item 13 — Tutorial: Proof of Cantor's Theorem

Content:
Let's now prove the theorem stated at the beginning of the lesson.

Content:
> The power set of a set [MATH: A] has a larger cardinality than [MATH: A,] i.e., [MATH: |A| < |\mathcal{P}(A)|.]

Content:
First, notice that [MATH: f: x \to \{x\}] injectively maps [MATH: A] into [MATH: \mathcal{P}(A).] So,

Content:
[MATH: |A| \leq \big| \mathcal{P}(A) \big|.]

Content:
To prove that no bijection exists between [MATH: A] and [MATH: \mathcal P(A),] we use proof by contradiction.

Content:
Suppose [MATH: g: A \to \mathcal{P}(A)] is a bijection of [MATH: A] onto [MATH: \mathcal{P}(A).] Note that if [MATH: x \in A,] then [MATH: g(x) \subseteq A.]

Content:
Next, we define

Content:
[MATH: S = \{ x \in A \mid x \notin g(x) \}.]

Content:
This set contains all elements of [MATH: A] that do not belong to their image under the action of [MATH: g.]

Content:
Now, since [MATH: S \subseteq A] and [MATH: g] is a bijection, there must be an element [MATH: y \in A] such that [MATH: g(y) = S.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ded758318a5d4c432602991ca6432946]

Content:
As a result, we have two mutually exclusive possibilities: [MATH: y \in S] or [MATH: y \notin S.]

Content:
- Case 1. Suppose [MATH: y \in S.] Then, by the definition of [MATH: S,] we have that [MATH: y \notin g(y) = S,] which is a contradiction.
- Case 2. Suppose [MATH: y \notin S.] Then, by the definition of [MATH: S,] we have that [MATH: y \in g(y) = S,] which is again a contradiction.

Content:
Either of these cases leads to a contradiction! This contradiction comes about by assuming that [MATH: g] is a bijection between [MATH: A] and [MATH: \mathcal{P}(A).] So, there are no bijections between these sets. Therefore, we conclude that

Content:
[MATH: |A| < \big| \mathcal{P}(A) \big|.]

Item 14 — Tutorial: The Continuum Hypothesis

Content:
As we know, [MATH: \aleph_0] is the "smallest" infinite cardinality, and [MATH: \aleph_0 < \mathfrak{c}.] But is there a set whose cardinality lies strictly between [MATH: \aleph_0] and [MATH: \mathfrak{c}?] In other words, is there a set [MATH: X] such that

Content:
[MATH: \aleph_0 < |X| < \mathfrak{c}?]

Content:
The assertion that no such set exists is called the continuum hypothesis.

Content:
It may surprise you that neither the continuum hypothesis nor its negation can be proved using the so-called standard axioms of set theory!

Content:
The challenge isn't that mathematicians can't prove the hypothesis because it's too difficult. Instead, a rigorous mathematical proof exists that neither the continuum hypothesis nor its negation can be proved!

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ec05ab8498d596ca37b3e3e4a6e0cf63]

Content:
This result might initially appear as a fundamental flaw in the very basics of mathematics. Although it might be unsettling, it's not the end of the world! Instead, it's the birth of two new worlds. This means that the continuum hypothesis (or its negation) should be taken as yet another axiom (a statement that we accept without proof). We do this in math quite often, especially at the beginning of any subject. An example from Euclidian geometry is the statement that exactly one line passes through two distinct points.

Content:
We obtain one mathematical framework if we accept the continuum hypothesis (CH) as true. If we assume the hypothesis is false (so, its negation is true), we arrive at a slightly different mathematical framework. However, both of these "mathematical worlds" are logically consistent. Most of the theorems in both worlds will remain the same, except for statements closely related to the continuum hypothesis. Whatever "world" we choose, it doesn't affect most things people want from math.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/8897d57f89ec2601ac855d2bac89a061]

Content:
This situation is not uncommon in mathematics. Another example is that we can have several valid "geometries" depending on the version of the axiom about parallel lines that we accept as true. Assuming that precisely one straight line passes through a point outside another line and is parallel to it, we get the "standard" Euclidean geometry in the plane. If we assume there can be infinitely many such parallel lines, we get hyperbolic geometry. And, if we assume there are no such parallel lines, we get spherical geometry. All three of these geometries are valid and have applications in different situations.
